title: Production Data Stack
body: When a number looks wrong — low utilization, a crusher stoppage, a drilling miss — pulling one workbook in isolation gets you a guess, not a cause. ADW's own history shows this: survey-vs-truck gaps get blamed on "reporting" when the real driver was loading position, and faults get flagged before anyone checked whether diesel burn already gave it away days earlier.
keyPoints: Four workbooks measure the same day at different depths: running-hours log (raw meter/diesel) → A&U (productive vs standby split) → daily report (KPI summary) → INX-SUM survey (independent ground-truth check). Each layer strips something the one below kept.

When a daily report number looks bad, read down the stack: daily report tells you what and roughly when, A&U tells you which unit and which reason code, running-hours log confirms the raw hours and names the operator, INX-SUM tells you if the fleet actually moved the ground or just logged loads.

A high truck count with a low survey number isn't automatically a counting or honesty problem — check loading position against the survey calculation area first. Ground moved outside the surveyed polygon reads as a gap that isn't one.
Diesel burn out of ratio with running hours in the raw log is an early fault signal — it shows up there before it becomes a breakdown line in A&U.
Don't conclude "underperformance" from one layer alone. The stack exists because no single workbook answers the whole question.
apply: If a unit's utilization or a block's tonnage looks off at the loading face or crusher feed, pull the running-hours log and A&U reason column before assuming it's an operator or equipment problem — the answer is usually sitting one layer down, not in the summary number itself.
